dek: An Indiana handicapper who started in the business in 1984 under a pen name and has run his own service, Team Stryker Sports, since 1999. His site sells football and basketball packages from $125 a week to $2,295 a year. All sales are final, and every record we found is a run chosen by the seller.

short_answer: Tom Stryker is a real, long running seller. His site names a company, Team Stryker Sports, gives a mailing address in Granger, Indiana and a toll free number, and lists prices for every package. A 2010 ESPN The Magazine feature describes him as the man who helped build and run the Buckeye Database, a private betting database once sold for $15,000 a copy. In that narrow sense the service is legitimate.

Whether the picks make money is a separate question, and nothing we could open answers it. The numbers on sale are runs he chose, such as a 15 and 2 record on NFL Games of the Year and a 59.6% record for Lee Stryker's club, plus two college football titles at The Sports Monitor in 2000 and 2001. The arithmetic in those claims is correct, but we found no full, time stamped log of every pick, and two of his own bios disagree with each other.

Treat Tom Stryker as an experienced seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. Season packages cost $495 to $1,495 and a year costs $2,295, all sales are final, and we found no guarantee and no independent buyer review, good or bad. If you buy, start with a week and record every pick yourself.

guarantee: We found no guarantee on any Team Stryker package page. The site terms say "All sales of “Digital Goods” are final," that a buyer is "waiving their rights to a return or refund" by purchasing, and that the company "will not provide the “Customer” with a refund for a cancellation that is part-way through a billing period." Subscriptions can be cancelled at any time in the My Account section, but the money for the current period is kept.

The terms are governed by "the law of England" with "the exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts," although the company address is in Indiana. That would make any dispute awkward for an American buyer. The Playbook page is headed "Today's Guaranteed Picks" but shows no terms explaining what is guaranteed. A buyer who loses money betting the picks gets nothing back, and betting losses are usually far larger than the package price.

claims_note: How we checked: we divided wins by wins plus losses (pushes left out) for every record that showed both numbers. All seven checked out to the rounding shown: 28 and 13 is 68.3%, 24 and 15 is 61.5%, 124 and 84 is 59.6%, 63 and 35 is 64.3%, 22 and 5 is 81.5%, 62 and 28 is 68.9%, and 49 and 25 is 66.2%. The math is honest. What the math cannot tell you is how many other runs, seasons and categories were left off the page.

The Game of the Year lines need care. The BigAl.com header claims 15 and 2 over 17 seasons from 2009 to 2025. The same page says his December 2019 Game of the Year was his 11th straight winner. If the first 11 years were all wins, the six seasons from 2020 to 2025 went 4 and 2, which is a good record but a much smaller and more recent sample than the headline suggests. No page lists the 17 games, so we could not check any of them.

The bios are not kept up to date and disagree on dates. The About page counts from 1984 and claims more than four decades; the BigAl.com bio still says 36 years; the CappersPicks bio says 25 years and "since 1984" at once. ESPN's 2010 article adds a detail the sales pages leave out: "Tom Stryker" is a pen name he took when he started working for Tom Scott in 1984, and his own service, Team Stryker Sports, opened in 1999. A VerifiedCappers bio says his first season as a pro was 1996. None of this is unusual in the business, but it means the start date in the marketing is the start of a career, not of a public record.
Dollar figures such as $44,550 assume a stake per rating that a buyer may not use. A 22 and 5 run on $2,000 plays is 27 bets, too few to judge anyone.
record: What a buyer can verify independently: very little. We found no full, time stamped log of every Tom Stryker pick with the line, the odds and the release time, no Sports Monitor results we could open, and no court, regulator or Better Business Bureau record about the service.

What we could confirm from outside his own sites: the 2010 ESPN The Magazine feature by Chad Millman describes Stryker as a man in his mid 40s living in Granger who played baseball at Indiana in the early 1980s, who entered most of the 600,000 plus data points in the Buckeye Database built by Tom Scott. ESPN says the database cost $15,000, had only nine owners, and covered NFL and college football from 1980 and pro and college basketball from 1990. The article also warns that a database "cannot answer a question it isn't asked" and that past results do not guarantee future ones. It reports no win and loss record for Stryker himself.

What sellers publish: product titles with ATS runs on teamstryker.com and BigAl.com, bios repeating the Sports Monitor titles, and a Playbook page with a "Tom's Last 10 Results" heading that showed no numbers when we looked on 20 Nov 2026. The homepage lists about 130 free plays from 8 Aug to 19 Nov 2026 with write ups but no graded results, so a buyer could grade them, though free plays may not match paid ones.

Results posted by others: Churchill Syndicate, an X account that sells its own packages, posted that Stryker went 2 and 1 on 1 Nov, 1 and 0 on 2 Nov and 3 and 0 on 8 Nov 2026. That is a reseller's marketing, not an audit, and three days of NFL sides prove nothing either way.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition no Tom Stryker pick history is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how Tom Stryker performs.
our_data.context: For scale: the runs in Tom Stryker sales copy go from 59.6% (124 and 84 for Lee's club) up to 81.5% on 27 whale plays. On the Watchdog board, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent buyer evidence on Tom Stryker is close to nil. We found no buyer review of a paid package, good or bad, on any forum, review site or app store. Our Reddit search was partial: the Reddit archive's full text search timed out or refused requests all day on 20 Nov 2026, as it had on 17 Nov, so we relied on our saved copy of r/sportsbook and r/sportsbetting posts from January 2024 to November 2026 and the comments of saved threads, which had nothing on him. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: We found nine items on five sites from 2010 to 2026, and none is a review of a paid Team Stryker package. The only discussion with any substance is a 2010 Sportsbook Review thread about free college football systems he had published: most replies were curious or encouraging, one doubted that systems with many conditions hold up, and the starter reported a 3, 1 and 1 first week. On TheRX his plays were reposted with the seller's own ATS titles in 2025, and since at least March 2023 the forum's rules have listed him on both its do not post lists, without a reason. The only results posts came from a reseller on X, all positive and all marketing. A review site that calls itself a monitor showed no reviews and no picks for him, and the Better Business Bureau had no listing. There is no smoke here either way: no pattern of complaints and no pattern of praise, just very little independent talk for a seller this old.

On Sportsbook Review, a member shared three college football systems that Stryker had given out as free tips, with records of 55 and 27, 188 and 103 and 108 and 156 ATS (the last one to bet against), and said he had started betting them. A week later he reported a 3, 1 and 1 week and said he would keep going. That is a tiny sample of free systems, not paid picks.

Replies in the same thread were split. Two members called the systems interesting or solid, one asked where the numbers came from, and one argued that systems with many conditions tend to look better in the past than they do going forward.

In a TheRX service play thread, a member reposted three Stryker college football plays with the seller's titles: a "36-16 ATS" high noon play on Texas, a "31-10 ATS" Saturday night play on Texas A&M and a "16-2 ATS" non conference best bet on Arizona. No lines were given and nobody posted how they did.

TheRX service play guidelines, posted in March 2023, list Tom Stryker (spelled with an extra y) under "Do not post these services" and again under "Do not post write-ups." The rules give no reason, and many well known sellers are on the same lists.

The same two listings were still in TheRX daily thread rules in March and August 2026. A web search snippet suggested he was on an allowed list, but the thread itself shows him only on the do not post lists.

Churchill Syndicate, an X account that sells packages and links to its own site, posted daily results that included Stryker at 2 and 1, 1 and 0, and 3 and 0 on three NFL days in early November 2026, quoting dollar wins at $1,000 a play. It is another seller's results post, not a buyer report.
VerifiedCappers, a site that calls itself a handicapping monitor and links to CappersPicks, showed 0 reviews and said "No sports picks have been posted" for Tom Stryker.

A Better Business Bureau search for Team Stryker Sports returned no business profile. Web searches found no Covers or Sportsbook Review buyer thread about his paid packages and no court or regulator record. Two Sportsbook Review service play threads from 2019 and 2020 that listed his plays now redirect to the forum home page and could not be read.

conflicts: Team Stryker sells picks from Big Al McMordie and Rocketman alongside Stryker's own, and BigAl.com sells Stryker's plays and hosts the ESPN article that praises both of them. ESPN says McMordie was one of the nine buyers of the database Stryker helped build. Each site's praise for the other is part of a business relationship.
Lee Stryker's High Roller Club is sold under the Team Stryker name, so his records are published by the same seller that profits from the sale.
The only results posts we found outside his own sites came from Churchill Syndicate, an X account that sells its own packages. That is marketing from another seller, not independent tracking.

A real, documented background: ESPN The Magazine profiled his role in building one of the best known betting databases.
The records he quotes add up: every win rate we recomputed matched the figure shown.
About 130 free plays with write ups were posted on the homepage from August to November 2026, so a buyer can watch and grade him before paying.
concerns: No full public record. Every number we saw is a run or season chosen by the seller, and some, like 22 and 5 on whale plays, are tiny samples.
All sales are final and we found no guarantee, even on packages costing $1,395 to $2,295.
Bios disagree from page to page (25, 36 and more than 40 years), and some copy is years out of date.
The terms are governed by English law and English courts, although the company address is in Indiana.
His plays are on TheRX's do not post lists, and we found no independent buyer review anywhere, so outside tracking is almost absent.
Single plays were not on sale on 20 Nov 2026, and the Playbook "Last 10 Results" box was empty, so even the seller side shows little current performance.
checklist: Ask Team Stryker for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds, the star rating and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Ask for the 17 NFL Games of the Year behind the 15 and 2 claim, with the line taken each year.
Grade the free homepage plays for a few weeks before you buy, using the line available when each was posted.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money, and dollar totals depend on the stake per star.
Start with the $125 week, not a season or year. All sales are final and partial periods are not refunded.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: He is a real, long running seller with a named company, an Indiana mailing address, a phone number and published prices, and ESPN The Magazine profiled his work on a well known betting database in 2010. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because he does not publish a full record of every pick, and we found no court or regulator action involving him.
How much does Tom Stryker cost?

On 20 Nov 2026 teamstryker.com sold football at $125 a week or $350 a month, basketball at $149 a week or $349 a month, season clubs from $495 to $1,495, a six month pass at $1,395 and a one year pass at $2,295. Single plays have sold at $30 but none of his were listed that day. Playbook sold a one day pass at $49.
Does Tom Stryker have a verified record?

No. The sales pages show runs such as 15 and 2 on NFL Games of the Year and Sports Monitor titles in 2000 and 2001. The percentages add up, but we found no independent, time stamped log of every pick, and no Watchdog graded record is matched to him.
Does Tom Stryker offer refunds or a guarantee?

No. The terms say all sales of digital goods are final, buyers waive any right to a refund, and cancelling part way through a billing period does not earn a refund. We found no guarantee on any package.

According to ESPN The Magazine, he lives in Granger, Indiana, played baseball at Indiana in the early 1980s, took the name Tom Stryker when he went to work for handicapper Tom Scott in 1984, helped build Scott's Buckeye Database, and opened his own service, Team Stryker Sports, in 1999.

You get a veteran's plays, written analysis and free picks to judge first. What is unproven is whether his picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of plays, and all sales are final, so a losing month costs you the fee as well as your bets. If you try him, buy a week, not a year.
